Hence, no testing was performed on the potentially improved membranes. 33 Identification of enzyme candidates (Task 5) One of the major bottlenecks in formate utilization was the inefficient conversion of formyl-CoA to formaldehyde coupled with 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA synthase (HACS). We use glycolate as a product proxy for the high-activity HACS screening. Compared with the ethylene glycol pathway, the biggest difference is the termination. We previously reported the conversion of formaldehyde to glycolic acid (glycolate) by E. coli resting cells overexpressing a HACS, an acyl-CoA reductase (ACR) that can oxidize formaldehyde to formyl-CoA and reduce glycolyl-CoA to glycolaldehyde, and an aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) that oxidizes glycolaldehyde to glycolate (Figure 26A). The experiments were conducted in 25-ml shake flasks with 5-10 ml working volume, which is not suitable for quantitative high throughput screens. Thus, we implemented 96 deep-well microtiter plate cultivations (1 ml reaction working volume) to improve the throughput for testing multiple variants, pathways, and relative expression levels of the pathway enzymes (Figure 26C). For better screening of HACS variants, we found the need to decouple the source for formaldehyde and formyl-CoA, which could be accomplished by generating formyl-CoA from formate via formate activation enzymes. There are multiple routes for formate activation: ATP-consuming formyl-CoA synthetases (FCS) or formate kinase- phosphoacyltransferase pairs (FOK-PTA), as well as acyl-CoA transferases (ACT) requiring specific CoA donor molecules. Among them, the ACT from Clostridium aminobutyricum (AbfT) was chosen for rapid screening of HACS activities as it can recycle CoA by utilizing glycolyl-CoA as a CoA donor (Figure 26A). Having a separate source for formyl-CoA generation via formate activation provides several advantages: (1) formyl-CoA flux is not affected by formaldehyde concentrations, hence allowing independent control of each HACS substrate; (2) only two enzymes need to be expressed for screening, which reduces genetic complexity in vivo; (3) formaldehyde consumption per glycolate production is reduced to 50% and uncoupled from in vivo formate production, which allows for a better estimation of kinetic parameters. As a host for screening, we used an engineered E. coli strain derived from MG1655(DE3) and containing knockouts for formaldehyde (∆frmA) and formate (∆fdhF ∆fdnG ∆fdoG) oxidation as well as for glycolate utilization (∆glcD), as these pathways could interfere with the analysis of the HACS-based pathway. Expression of HACS and AbfT are controlled independently using orthogonal inducible promoters, HACS under an IPTG-inducible T7 promoter, and AbfT under a cumate- inducible T5 promoter system (Figure 27B). Optimization of relative expression levels by exploring different levels of IPTG and cumate concentrations was previously demonstrated to have a substantial impact on pathway flux. In addition, we investigated varying formaldehyde concentrations to examine the impact on FORCE pathway flux using previously identified HACS, RuHACS.
